az_first_jacuzzi_spire.blurb: The biggest of three granite spires in a quiet backcountry pocket north of Phoenix, and the first one you meet on the walk in. It holds 11 mostly trad lines, a few of them multi-pitch, with two bolted sport routes mixed in. Grades range from a fourth-class scramble through easy and moderate 5.7 to 5.9 terrain, with a handful of 5.10 and 5.11 leads at the top end. The walk finishes with a steep, loose scree scramble to the base. One side of the spire sits in shade for most of the day while the opposite face bakes in sun, so you can pick a face to suit the temperature.

az_tri_level_spire.blurb: A granite spire on Mount Lemmon near the Windy Point overlook, outside Tucson, at roughly 6,000 feet. It has 11 climbs, split between six trad lines and five sport routes. The grades lean hard: most are in the 5.11 range, with one 5.12 and only a few lines at 5.9 to 5.10 or easier. Routes are spread over both sides of the formation, so you can usually find either shade or sun depending on the day. The pullout parking is close, though the final stretch down to the base is a careful scramble on a slope.

az_morrell_s_wall_parking_lot.blurb: A cluster of granite boulder piles in the McDowell Mountains above Scottsdale, perched on a saddle on the way up to the wall that gives the area its name. The piles stand roughly 40 to 75 feet tall and offer 10 routes, mostly trad with a couple of bolted lines. Difficulty is modest: a scrambly easy traverse, a run of 5.7 to 5.9 climbs and one 5.10. The walk from the main trailhead is short, around 10 to 15 minutes along a few connecting trails and across a wash, which makes it a handy half-day stop for newer leaders.

_expect.name: Old Man Stone Face and Hollin Walls

az_old_man_stone_face_and_hollin_walls.blurb: Two small granite walls in the Bear Canyon section of Mount Lemmon, near Tucson, reached by a walk of about 20 to 25 minutes up from the highway. The old man face is the first wall, with Hollin Wall a little farther east. The ten routes, eight of them trad and two sport, mostly sit at 5.9, with a few easier and harder options up to 5.11. Climbs are short, at most around 75 feet, so a single rope covers it. Lines begin close together and fan out higher up. Most routes face south, so the pocket warms up nicely on cold days.

az_mars_roof.blurb: A large double roof of limestone in Priest Draw, a grassy bouldering valley near Flagstaff at about 7,000 feet. It is one of the farthest features in the draw, around a 20 minute walk up the main trail, and nothing lies beyond it. The ten problems here are all very hard, from the V10 range up into V13, so this is a destination for strong boulderers rather than a place to warm up. Several lines start from one spot under the lower roof and split to different headwall finishes, and a link-up joins the lower and upper roofs.
